issues.legal_issue: A right of prior purchase based on a common outer entrance does not require that the entrance be jointly owned by the owners of the properties.
material_facts: The claimant sought prior purchase of a house sold to the appellant, relying on the common outer entrance shared by her house and the sold house.
The courts below found on the evidence that both houses had a common outer entrance and access over a private passage; the passage was owned by others, not jointly by the owners of the houses.
The appellant argued that the right could arise only if the claimant and the purchaser jointly owned the common entrance.
issues.conclusion: The statutory right of prior purchase based on a common outer entrance does not depend on joint ownership of that entrance by the owners of the properties.
issues.legal_principle: The plain language of section 15(fourthly) of the Right of Prior Purchase Act, 1993 requires a common outer entrance but does not require that the owners of the properties jointly own it. Whether a common outer entrance exists depends on the facts proved in each case. The court distinguished the cited Punjab decisions, including Naba v. Piara Mal, Nanak Chand v. Tek Chand, Asa Nand v. Mahmud, and Ram Chand v. Ram Jowaya, as turning on their particular facts.

predicates.property_sale_preemption_claim: A claim for prior purchase is made in connection with the sale of a property.
predicates.claimant_and_sold_properties_have_common: The property of the claimant and the property sold share a common outer entrance.
predicates.joint_ownership_requirement_is_contested: A party argues that the owners of the properties must jointly own the common outer entrance for the prior-purchase claim to succeed.

issues.definition: When a prior-purchase claim arises from a property sale, the properties share a common outer entrance, and joint ownership is contested, the claim does not require the property owners to jointly own that entrance.

issues.legal_issue: A right of prior purchase for properties sharing a common outer entrance is a reasonable restriction on the purchaser's property right.
material_facts: The sale concerned a house whose owners and the claimant's house owners had access through a common passage and outer entrance.
The passage was private property, and the owners of houses opening onto it had rights of way over it.
The appellant argued that the prior-purchase provision imposed an unreasonable restriction on the right to property.
issues.conclusion: The restriction imposed by the prior-purchase provision for properties sharing a common outer entrance is reasonable and constitutionally valid.
issues.legal_principle: The court applied Article 19(1)(f) of the Constitution and followed Bhau Ram v. Baijnath, which upheld analogous grounds of pre-emption for co-sharers, owners of common staircases, and owners of properties with a common entrance. Owners of buildings sharing a common entrance stand more or less in the position of co-sharers, making the restriction sustainable. The court also referred to Bishan Singh v. Khazan Singh for the nature of pre-emption as a right of substitution, and to Govind Dayal v. Inayatullah for the description of that right.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_property_pre: A party challenges the constitutionality of a restriction imposed through a right of prior purchase of property.
predicates.property_sale_preemption_claim: A claim for prior purchase is made in connection with the sale of a property.
predicates.properties_share_common_entrance_and_acc: The properties share a common entrance and access through a passage.

issues.definition: When a property-prior-purchase rule is constitutionally challenged in a sale proceeding involving properties that share a common entrance and access, the restriction is reasonable.
